event: Elsie wakes at half past four in her crown and shawl. On the sill Moonpenny is still open.
She tells Moonpenny good morning. It's the twenty-first. Today is the house.
She counts it on her fingers like Tamsin does: pay at dawn, Coin Street at eight, four suns.
She lays the birch crown on the sill by Moonpenny, keeps the shawl on, and pins her clip.

changes.note: Elsie lays her birch crown on the sill by Moonpenny

event: In the bee tin under its cloth, two honey cakes are left over from the boat.
Downstairs the oven is lit and Mrs Merriweather is at the peel, sliding out the first loaves.
Elsie asks to warm one cake on the oven ledge. It's promised to a man on Coin Street, warm.
Mrs Merriweather sets it on the ledge herself. She says two minutes. Not three.
She asks how the boat went. Elsie says thieves, and a bell, and Moonpenny opened.
Mrs Merriweather grunts at the thieves. At Moonpenny she nods, slower.
Elsie wraps the warm cake in a cloth and tucks it inside the shawl, against her middle.
At ten to five the Lantern Steps are grey with mist. The Mere is white. The lanterns are out.
The steps are strewn with burnt-out lanterns. Gulls walk among them, picking at the nut paper.
Ines sits halfway down, alone, with Biscuit asleep on her feet.
Elsie sits by her. Ines whispers that this is her favourite hour. She came back for it.
Ines asks, very low, whether the boat sank. Elsie says no, and tells how Noor threw the vial.
Ines says Biscuit wouldn't come home last night until Noor stood up. He'd have stayed till dawn.
Cora comes down through the mist in her grey gloves, the lavender still at her throat.
Elsie asks if her hands are warm. Cora flexes them in the grey wool. She says they are.
Tamsin comes down, crown crooked, curls wet with mist. She didn't sleep. Rooms don't move.
Tilly comes yawning, holding a wool sock that sags and clinks. Her savings. All of them.
Tamsin asks why a sock. Tilly says her purse has a hole, and the sock hasn't. Yet.
Noor comes last along the waterfront, out of the mist. She sits one step above them.
Biscuit wakes, climbs off Ines's feet, and goes and sits on Noor's boots instead.
At five Odile Marsh comes up from her boat with a strongbox under one arm and her slate.
She pays the guard boats one by one by their numbers. Eleven is last.
She counts twelve silver lanterns into Elsie's cupped hands. They're cold and wet from the mist.

changes.note: Odile pays eleven twelve silver lanterns into Elsie's hands: 190 → 310
Elsie gains 50 XP for the E-rank barge guard (60 → 110 / 350)
Tamsin gains 50 XP for the E-rank barge guard (530 → 580)
Tilly gains 50 XP for the E-rank barge guard (210 → 260)

event: Odile says the thief who couldn't swim is in the watch house, and has named the other three.
She says she'll send the guild a chit: eleven did well. She wants eleven again next year.
She looks at Noor. She says: at the back again. Noor says, maybe. Odile goes down to her boat.
Elsie holds the twelve lanterns out on her palms. Tamsin starts dividing shares on her fingers.
Tamsin says five into twelve doesn't go. She tries again. It still doesn't go.
Cora says a Warden is paid by the guild. She takes no share. She says it to the mist.

changes.note: Bond: Cora 63 → 64 (kindness: she takes no share, so it goes to the house)

event: Noor says she said on the water: hers goes to the house. She isn't taking it back.
Tilly says then all twelve go to the house, and tips her sock out on the step.
They pile it all on the stone: Elsie's purse, Tamsin's, Tilly's sock and the twelve lanterns.
Tilly sorts it into stacks of ten pips, fast, lips moving. Tamsin watches her hands, lost.
Tilly sits back. Four suns, and eight pips over. She counts again to be sure. Eight over.

changes.note: Bond: Tilly 62 → 63 (kindness: her whole sock of savings tipped in for the house)

event: Tilly says without Noor's share and Cora's they'd have been forty pips short.
Tamsin whoops. A gull goes up off the step, and the mist swirls.
Elsie hugs Noor round the neck from behind. Noor says, the step, into the shawl.
Elsie hugs Cora next. Cora goes stiff, then pats her back once with a grey glove.
They sweep it all into the sock. Tamsin ties it and shoves it inside her jerkin. Nobody robs her.
Noor says she's going to bed. Elsie asks her to Coin Street first, to see where her coin goes.
Noor looks at the lump in Tamsin's jerkin. She says she'd like to see the door. Just the door.
Elsie asks Ines to supper tonight, at the blue door on Willow Canal. Ines looks startled. She nods.
Ines goes up the steps toward Ash Lane with Biscuit on her shoulder.
Three hours till eight. Tamsin says breakfast. Tilly says eight pips. Tamsin says a loaf, then.
At a stall at the top of the steps Tamsin buys a loaf with one pip from the sock. Seven over now.
They eat it walking the canals as the mist lifts, torn in five, Noor at the end of the row.
On Willow Canal they stand on the walk across from the blue door. Nobody says anything.
The blue paint is peeling. The fish knocker is green with age. A cat sleeps on the step.
Noor looks at it a long time. She says: it's a door. It stays where it is. Elsie says yes.
Tamsin says she'll have a room over the water. She has said so every day since the eighth.
Tilly says the shed, and the room beside Elsie's, so they can knock goodnight through the wall.
Elsie looks up at Cora. Cora says she has not been asked. Elsie says she's being asked. Now.
Cora looks at the door a long moment. She says she will consider it. She touches the lavender.
The cat on the step stretches and walks off. Tamsin says even the cat's moving out for them.
At ten to eight Coin Street lies in shade. The letting agent's door is still shut.
Elsie feels the cake inside her shawl. It's still warm. Nearly.
Four adventurers in good mail turn into the far end of the street, walking fast. C-rank tags.
Tamsin says that's them, the C-rank lot. After Midsummer, they said. It's after Midsummer.
The tower clock begins to strike eight. Tilly says that's her father's clock. The bolt draws back.
Tamsin pulls the door open and holds it. Elsie goes in first, and the rest crowd in behind.
The agent looks up from his heaps of keys. Elsie sets the warm cake on his desk. She promised.
He unwraps it and looks at it, warm in the cloth, as if nobody had brought him anything in years.
Tamsin sets the sock on the desk. Four suns, she says. In pips, mostly. Sorry.
The C-rank leader comes in behind them, a tall woman with a fat purse. She says: the blue door.
The agent says, kindly, first come. He nods at the sock. She looks at it, and at Elsie's hair.
She says: the Enthraller's lot. Tamsin folds her arms and says: the Fairweather party.
The tall woman shrugs. Plenty of houses. She goes out. Tilly lets out a breath like a kettle.
The agent counts the pips into heaps. It takes a long time. Noor waits by the door, very still.
A ring of keys slides off the desk. Then the whole heap goes, in a long jingling avalanche.
Noor says flatly: that was me. The agent, down on his knees, says it happens every day.
Elsie kneels to help gather. One key with a blue paper tag has slid right up to her boot.
The agent finishes: four suns, exact. He pushes back seven pips. Tilly puts them in the sock.
He writes in his book: four suns, a month's rent and one in hand. Two suns due on the first.
Tamsin's face falls: the first is ten days off. Two suns in ten days. Elsie says: notices.
He takes the blue-tagged key from Elsie, writes on its tag, and closes her fingers round it.
He bites the honey cake. He says it's warm. It's exactly as warm as she said it would be.
Out on Coin Street Elsie holds the key up to the sun. Tamsin lifts her off her feet and spins her.
Cora says she is due at the hall and late. She will come this evening, to see the sills.
Noor says she has seen the door now and will sleep. Elsie says supper. Noor says: ask me tonight.
Elsie, Tamsin and Tilly run all the way to Willow Canal, Tilly's sock jingling.
Elsie puts the key in the blue door. It sticks. Tamsin leans on it. It opens with a groan.
The kitchen is one long room: a scrubbed table, a black iron range, a stone sink. Dust in the sun.
Six chairs stand round the table, none of them matching. Elsie counts them, touching each back.
Tilly opens the back door on the garden: long grass, poppies, brambles, the leaning apple tree.
Tilly runs down through the grass to the shed and looks in. She shrieks. It has shelves.
The back sills face south and the sun is already on them. Elsie can see her plants on them.
Up the stairs is a parlour over the canal, with a green sofa that sags in the middle.
Tamsin goes straight to the parlour window and pushes it open. The canal is right below.
She leans out on her forearms. A punt goes by under her. She stays leaning there, saying nothing.
Behind the parlour is one small bedroom with a bare bedstead, its ropes laced across.
At the top are two small rooms under the roof slope, side by side. One has a gable window.
Tilly goes in one and knocks three times on the wall. Elsie, in the other, knocks back three.
Elsie takes the gable room, Tilly the one beside. Tamsin takes the room behind the parlour.
Tamsin asks, quieter, where Cora would go. Elsie says they'll find somewhere. There's the sofa.
There are no mattresses, only ropes. Tamsin says they've slept on worse. Tilly says she hasn't.
They part to fetch their things: Tamsin toward the docks, Tilly to Pickle Row.
Elsie walks back to Thimble Canal alone, holding the key in her pocket the whole way.
Mrs Merriweather is at the counter. Elsie sets the bee tin down, washed. She's found a house.
She tells her the blue door all in a rush. Mrs Merriweather listens with her arms folded.
Elsie says she'll pay for the attic to the end of the week. Mrs Merriweather says the week's paid.
Mrs Merriweather pushes the bee tin back across the counter. Keep it. For the honey cakes.
She takes a loaf off the rack and puts it in the tin. She grunts. It's a low grunt.
Elsie's eyes fill. She leans over the counter and hugs her, flour and all. She gets two pats.
Mrs Merriweather says the oven's cool by four on Sundays, if she wants to bake. Elsie says yes.
Elsie tells her where: Willow Canal, the blue door, mind the step. In case anyone asks for her.
In the attic Elsie packs the crate: Captain, Sunny, Doris, Mrs Pennywhistle, the shawl on top.
Moonpenny can't go in the crate, open as she is. Elsie will carry her in her arms.
She looks round: the round window, the narrow bed, the splinters. She thanks the room out loud.
Tamsin's voice comes up from the street. She's back with her bag, and Margery.
Tamsin carries the crate down two flights on one shoulder. Elsie follows with Moonpenny.
At Willow Canal Tilly sits on the step with a carpetbag and a crate of copper pipe.
Tilly says her landlady helped carry the copper down, singing. Pleased to see the back of it.
Elsie puts a plant on every sill. Captain goes on the kitchen sill. Moonpenny goes in the parlour.
Tilly carries her copper down to the shed. She stands inside and lays her palm flat on the bench.
Tamsin lights the range. Smoke pours out of every crack, and the kitchen goes grey.
They run coughing into the garden. Tamsin says, the flue. Tilly says a sweep costs. Seven pips.
Tamsin ties the yard broom to a clothes pole and climbs out onto the roof with it.
The broom goes halfway down the chimney and sticks. Tamsin swears at it. It stays stuck.
They eat Mrs Merriweather's loaf in the long grass under the apple tree, with nothing on it.
Tilly lies back in the grass, braids spread. She's never lived anywhere with a tree.
Tamsin lies on Elsie's other side. Elsie is in the middle, in the poppies, looking up at leaves.
Tilly's hand finds Elsie's in the grass. Tamsin sees it, and looks away at the sky.
Elsie says this is the best day. Better than Midsummer, even. She's sure.
Elsie dozes off in the sun with Tilly's hand in hers and Tamsin's shoulder at her other side.
She wakes at four with an apple leaf on her cheek. Tilly picks it off, laughing.
Tamsin is gone from the grass. There's banging in the kitchen. She's scrubbing the table.
They scrub the house: Tilly the sink, Elsie the sills, Tamsin the floor on her knees.
At the scrubbed table Elsie writes her mother: a house, a blue door, six chairs, a tree.
She writes the new address at the bottom twice, so her mother can't miss it.
At six Ines comes to the blue door with Biscuit and a crock of honey.
Ines whispers that a house should have honey. She sets it in the middle of the table.
Biscuit goes to the cold range, climbs into the oven through its open door, and curls up.
At half past six Amara is on the step with a big covered basket. Mrs Merriweather told her.
The basket has cold chicken, a pie, cherries, and a cake left from her mother's Midsummer table.
Elsie hugs her. Amara holds on. She whispers into Elsie's hair: I sang.
Elsie says she knows. She wasn't listening. She was washing a bowl. Very hard. Her eyes fill.
Amara laughs and her eyes fill too. She looked for the pink, and found it when the bell rang.
Amara says her mother cried on the barge, after. She'd never once seen her mother cry.
Amara looks at Elsie's mouth while Elsie wipes her eyes. Then away, at the six chairs.
At seven Noor comes to the door with a black iron coffee pot. It's tonight. She was asked.
Tamsin, sooty from the roof, says the range smokes. The broom's stuck up the flue.
Noor goes to the range to set down her pot. She stands by it a moment.
Deep in the chimney something cracks. Soot comes down in a great black fall, and the broom.
It billows over Tamsin, crouched at the hearth. She's black from her curls to her belt.
Noor says flatly: things break near me. Tamsin, spitting soot, says: and unbreak.
Tilly lights the range. It draws. The flame goes straight up the clean flue. No smoke at all.
At the stone sink Elsie scrubs the soot off Tamsin's face with a wet cloth, freckle by freckle.
Tamsin holds still with her eyes shut while Elsie washes round her mouth. Her ears go red.
Noor sets her coffee pot on the range. She says: so there's coffee. When I come.
At half past seven the fish knocker goes three times, exactly. It's Cora.
She has a pot of lavender under her arm, grown and in flower. She says it is for a sill.
Elsie puts it on the kitchen sill beside Captain. She names it Ledger. Cora's mouth twitches.
Cora looks round: plants on every sill, the honey, Noor's coffee pot, Biscuit in the oven.
Supper: seven of them, six chairs. Elsie turns her empty plant crate up at the corner.
Tamsin offers her chair. Tilly offers hers. Amara half rises. Elsie says she likes the crate.
They eat Amara's basket and Ines's honey. Noor pours coffee for anyone who'll have it.
Cora drinks Noor's coffee and says it wants one sugar. Noor says it does not.
Tamsin tells the thieves with her arms. Tilly does the bang. Biscuit purrs in the oven.
Elsie looks down the table at them in the lamplight. Seven. Her eyes fill. Tamsin passes a napkin.
Cora opens her ledger at the table, writes a line, and turns it so Elsie can read without asking.
It reads: Willow Canal. Supper. Skills used, none.
At ten Cora stands. She'll walk Noor home to Wick Lane. It's on her way. Noor says it is.
At the door Elsie asks Cora again, quietly, about the sofa. Cora says the Accord is silent on sofas.
Then she says: perhaps. Not tonight. She touches the lavender at her throat and goes.
Noor says from the step: tomorrow, then. Not ask me tomorrow. Only tomorrow. She goes.
Amara and Ines go off together toward Lantern Square, Biscuit riding on Ines's shoulder.
The kitchen goes quiet: three of them, the range ticking, Captain and Ledger on the sill.
Tilly goes up first. Elsie hears her climb two flights, and the bed ropes creak.
In the gable room Elsie lies on her blanket on the bed ropes. The window is full of stars.
Three knocks come through the wall. Elsie knocks three back. Tilly laughs through the wall.
Under her breastbone the thread to Tamsin is awake and restless, like fingers drumming.
Elsie goes down in the dark. Tamsin isn't in her room. She's on the green sofa in the parlour.
She lies by the open window, awake, listening to the canal. She says rooms still don't move.
Elsie says the water does. She sits on the sofa, and it sags them together into the middle.
Tamsin laughs low. The sofa won't let them apart. Elsie leans on her. Tamsin's arm comes round.
Tilly comes to the doorway with her blanket, braids down. She says the wall went quiet.
She looks at the two of them a moment. Then she climbs on the sofa's other end, feet under Elsie.
Over Elsie's head Tamsin and Tilly look at each other. Tilly lifts her chin. Tamsin nods once.
Tilly spreads her blanket over all three of them. The sofa sags further. Nobody moves.
Elsie falls asleep between them, the canal going by under the window, the thread warm and still.
